intro: The Rondo-Burleske, marked Allegro assai. Sehr trotzig, is the third movement of the Ninth Symphony and gives virtuoso writing to the whole orchestra, with angular themes overlapping at speed. In the middle section a trumpet plays a melody in D major that returns in the finale.

sections.label: A · Trumpet calls and jagged strings
sections.mNote: Short figures combine into the rondo’s contrapuntal lines.

sections.label: B · Trumpet melody in D major
sections.mNote: Held strings under a trumpet melody with a small turn figure.

sections.label: B′ · Harp sweeps and tremolos
sections.mNote: Harp sweeps and string tremolos separate the sharp exchanges.

sections.label: A′ · Return of the rondo theme
sections.mNote: The opening figures return and continue to the close.

sections.label: Coda · Più stretto, then Presto
sections.mNote: Short orchestral figures lead to an abrupt close in A minor.

cues.title: Opening, solo trumpet
cues.text: The first trumpet plays a short figure alone in the first bar, and Mahler marks the movement Allegro assai. Sehr trotzig (very defiant). Strings follow with jagged figures, and horns and woodwinds add short figures of their own. The violins then take up the main melody at ff.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, Universal Edition first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 104: Allegro assai. Sehr trotzig; first trumpet alone in the first bar, string, horn and woodwind figures, the violins’ melody ff. Bettie Jo Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: chromatic fragments in the brass introduce the refrain, sehr trotzig, and the violins then take up the main melody: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Dedication “to my brothers in Apollo”
cues.text: Mahler dedicated the movement, derisively, “to my brothers in Apollo”, meaning his fellow disciples of the god of music.
cues.evidence: Reinhold Kubik’s note for Universal Edition describes the Rondo-Burleske as derisively dedicated to my brothers in Apollo: https://www.universaledition.com/en/Mahler-Symphony-No.-9-Original-draft-of-1st-3-Movements.-Facsimile-of-Composers-Manuscript-D-major-for-orchestra/P0005537

cues.title: First episode
cues.text: The first episode has reduced scoring, softer dynamics and one flat in the key signature, and its melodic lines draw on the style of operetta. The refrain’s dissonance continues underneath.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 111–114: one flat, reduced scoring. Basinger: the first episode keeps the refrain’s dissonance and some of its contrapuntal sophistication, but the reduced scoring and softer dynamic level brighten the tone, and the melodic lines channel the style of operetta and other popular music of the period: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Vienna before the Anschluss, 1938
cues.text: This performance took place in January 1938. Two months later Nazi Germany annexed Austria. Walter, already driven from Germany because he was Jewish, had to leave his adopted country too, and Mahler’s music disappeared from its concert programmes.
cues.evidence: Erik Ryding, Library of Congress essay, p. 2, on the recording, Anschluss, Walter’s exile and suppression of Mahler’s music. https://lcweb2.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: Muted trumpet with triangle roll
cues.text: The muted first trumpet plays twice, ff with an immediate diminuendo. Under it the triangle holds a roll with a crescendo, and the violins play repeated notes.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 123: first trumpet mit Dämpfer, ff dim.; triangle roll with crescendo; violins on repeated notes.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bruno Walter on the movement, 1936
cues.text: In 1936 Bruno Walter described this movement as “defiantly agitated” and called it the “most striking proof” of Mahler’s contrapuntal mastery.
cues.evidence: Walter’s Gustav Mahler (1936), quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: Episode in D major, solo trumpet
cues.text: A cymbal stroke halts the fugue. Brass chords play a dissonant chorale, and at Etwas gehalten the music moves to D major. A solo trumpet, marked p subito poco espressivo, plays a melody built on turn figures over string tremolo; the turn motive returns in the finale’s main melody.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 132: Beck. stroke, flutes Flatterzunge, brass chords, Etwas gehalten, two sharps, trumpet p subito poco espressivo over string tremolo pp subito. Basinger: a cymbal crash halts the imitative process, the second episode begins with a dissonant chorale from the preceding fugue and then a lyrical melody full of turn motives and sigh figures; the finale’s primary melody absorbs the turn motive of the Rondo-Burleske: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Gaisberg and Walter, Paris
cues.text: A few weeks after the concert, Fred Gaisberg met Walter in Paris to play him the test pressings. Gaisberg described Walter as “a bewildered refugee”. Walter was “so delighted” with the results that his “usually sober face brightened up considerably”.
cues.evidence: Gaisberg’s 1944 account, quoted in Erik Ryding’s Library of Congress essay: https://www.loc.gov/static/programs/national-recording-preservation-board/documents/MahlerSymphonyNo9.pdf

cues.title: Harp glissandos and divided violins
cues.text: Fragments of the rondo return several times within the song. Each time a harp glissando cuts them off, and the violins are left playing am Steg, near the bridge, in divided parts.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 141: harp glissandos, second violins 3fach geteilt, am Steg, pp, immer Dämpfer in the horns.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Lyrical melody and rondo fragments
cues.text: The music darkens. The oboe, followed by other instruments, repeatedly plays the lyrical melody, but in the end the orchestra does not take it up, and fragments of the rondo return.
cues.evidence: Basinger’s Utah Symphony guide: the mood darkens as a clarinet gruffly anticipates the refrain; the oboe, followed by other instruments, keeps trying to reinstate the lyrical melody, and the orchestra ultimately rejects it: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/

cues.title: Coda, Più stretto and Presto
cues.text: The closing pages are marked Più stretto, then Presto. Winds, brass and strings repeat the short figures of the opening with heavy accents. The movement ends on short, sharp attacks like those at its start.
cues.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), pp. 157–163: Più stretto on p. 157, short repeated figures in winds, brass and strings at ff, final short attacks on p. 163. Basinger: the refrain resurfaces and the Rondo-Burleske ends in the same ill-humour in which it opened: https://usuo.org/explore/2016/05/mahler-9-listening-guide/
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Cymbal stroke, chorale and D major
transitions.from: A · Trumpet calls and jagged strings
transitions.to: B · Trumpet melody in D major
transitions.how: A cymbal stroke halts the imitative writing. Flutter-tongued flutes and tremolo strings continue, the brass play a dissonant chorale, and at Etwas gehalten the harmony moves to D major under a solo trumpet.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 132. Basinger: a cymbal crash halts the imitative process; a dissonant chorale precedes the lyrical melody.

transitions.title: Harp glissando leads to string tremolo
transitions.from: B · Trumpet melody in D major
transitions.how: The broad melody breaks into short phrases passed between instruments. Fragments of the rondo theme enter, and a harp glissando follows. The strings then return to the tremolo am Steg, marked pp.
transitions.evidence: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, UE first-edition full score (Dover reprint, IMSLP353450), p. 141: harp glissandos, string tremolo am Steg pp.

transitions.title: The short figures accelerate
transitions.from: A′ · Return of the rondo theme
transitions.how: The tempo increases to Più stretto and later to Presto. Strings, winds and brass play the short opening motifs in close succession, and the percussion doubles their accents. The movement ends on A minor chords.
transitions.evidence: Universal Edition score, pp. 157–163, tempo markings and final A-minor chords.

source.title: Mahler, Symphony No. 9, first-edition full score (Universal Edition, 1912; Dover reprint)
source.locator: Movement III, printed pp. 104–163: opening trumpet call; D-major trumpet melody in the central episode; E♭-clarinet interruptions; accelerating close on pp. 157–163.

timeline.note: A solo trumpet plays the first short call before the strings answer.
Jagged string figures and horn calls cross rising lines in the woodwind and low strings.
The solo trumpet plays a melody in D major over tremolo strings.
Clarinets sharpen the melody’s turn; harp sweeps interrupt the returning rondo fragments.
Trombones and low strings restore the opening theme.
Short figures pass quickly through the orchestra, with timpani and percussion reinforcing the accents.

fields.label: Catalogue

fields.label: Matrix, take, sides

The inspected DAHR composer listing did not establish a matrix/take match for this digital source; no exhaustive absence is claimed. Specific takes and a verified movement-to-matrix mapping remain unestablished, so the complete-set series is not presented as a side identification for this file.

fields.label: Transfer
fields.note: No engineer for the source CD or Commons transfer is identified. Gaisberg was the original recording producer and Charlie Gregory the recording engineer, not established digital-transfer credits. Andrew Rose’s named 2013 Pristine transfer is a different reissue and is not the source of this Commons upload.

fields.label: Transfer date
fields.note: No transfer date is established. The embedded digitising value 1962 is not corroborated as a transfer date and is not used as one; neither upload nor release dates substitute for it.

fields.note: Mahler died in 1911. This is a term calculation for the composition, not worldwide clearance of an unidentified edition or transfer.

fields.note: The inspected template expressly concerns expired performer and producer rights in the European Union. This package is admitted on that territorial recording-rights basis, not merely the composition’s age. United States status is not established; no worldwide public-domain clearance is asserted.

composer.epithet: Conductor who composed during the summers and intended each symphony to contain a whole world, combining the sublime with the music of the street band.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. In Iglau he heard bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church, and these sounds recur throughout his music. Late in life he told Sigmund Freud that he had once run from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was playing Ach, du lieber Augustin.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, where he studied piano and composition, and he sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. Among his friends were Hugo Wolf and Hans Rott, who died young. Rott’s symphony is so close to Mahler’s own music that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. By then he had already begun his career as a conductor.
